video_title: The Bitcoin Truth Wall Street Doesn't Want You to Hear
gist: Despite a title framed around Bitcoin and Wall Street, this is an operator interview with Nancy Beaton, president of retail at Uphold, on what crypto retail users actually demand: not self-custody purism but yield, collateralized borrowing, one-step asset swaps and crypto IRAs. Beaton argues digital assets are converging into ordinary financial portfolios, that regulatory clarity (the Clarity Act) mainly unblocks regulated banks/broker-dealers rather than retail, and that tokenized securities will arrive but slower than the hype implies. Uphold's strategic pivot is toward white-labeling its API'd platform to banks and fintechs.

insights.claim: Uphold's retail president argues crypto is no longer 'outside the system' because customer demand — not institutional evangelism — is what pulled BlackRock, Fidelity and banks in, and digital assets are becoming a standard line item in ordinary financial portfolios.
insights.speaker: Nancy Beaton (president of retail, Uphold)
insights.so_what: Frames the industry's growth driver as retail pull rather than institutional push — favors platforms that own the end-user relationship over pure infrastructure plays.
insights.quote: I think customer demand is what is prompting people to bring digital assets into the fold and give people access to digital assets.

insights.claim: Crypto-native user expectations — instant, borderless, 24/7, cheap settlement — are now being imposed by consumers back onto equities and traditional financial instruments, creating pressure on legacy rails rather than the reverse.
insights.speaker: Nancy Beaton (president of retail, Uphold)
insights.so_what: Watch for T+0/24-7 settlement initiatives at incumbent brokers; incumbents that can't match crypto UX face structural attrition of younger accounts.
insights.quote: Consumers want their money to move like emails. They want it to be borderless, they want it to be frictionless, they want it to be cheaper.

insights.claim: Pompliano notes BlackRock's single largest and most profitable product is now its Bitcoin ETF, making the world's biggest asset manager effectively a crypto company by revenue mix even though it would never brand itself that way.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano (host)
insights.so_what: If accurate, BlackRock's earnings sensitivity to Bitcoin price and ETF flows is far higher than its equity narrative implies.
insights.quote: If you look at, take BlackRock as an example, their largest, most profitable product is the Bitcoin ETF.

insights.claim: Enterprise adoption of digital assets is being driven by banks and fintechs wanting to 'plug-and-play' crypto into existing applications to meet customer demand, rather than building crypto capability in-house.
insights.speaker: Nancy Beaton (president of retail, Uphold)
insights.so_what: Bullish for B2B crypto-infrastructure and white-label wallet vendors that sell into regulated distribution.

themes.theme: What retail users actually want: yield, credit, one-step swaps

insights.claim: Uphold's user research says the dominant retail demand is no longer buying more crypto but doing more with already-accumulated holdings — borrowing against them, lending them out, and earning yield without selling.
insights.speaker: Nancy Beaton (president of retail, Uphold)
insights.so_what: The retail growth market is crypto-collateralized credit and yield products, not incremental spot trading volume — relevant to exchange revenue-mix forecasts.
insights.quote: They want to borrow against them, they want to be able to lend them out, they want to be able to earn on the asset portfolio that they've been building over these years.

insights.claim: Uphold has built a stack of collateralized products: borrowing against crypto to a Visa signature card, USDC lending for yield via the Exactly protocol, and — launching this week — a cash lump-sum loan collateralized by XRP, BTC, ETH or USDC.
insights.speaker: Nancy Beaton (president of retail, Uphold)
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that DeFi lending protocols are being embedded as back-ends for regulated retail apps; watch Exactly-style protocols for distribution-driven TVL.
insights.quote: This week we are launching borrow, so you can get what feels like more of a traditional loan where you put your assets up as collateral, your XRP, your BTC, your ETH, your USDC

insights.claim: Uphold has launched fractional equities with roughly 4,000 stocks and ETFs, minimum $5, allowing a direct one-step swap between Bitcoin and Apple or Tesla without routing through dollars.
insights.speaker: Nancy Beaton (president of retail, Uphold)
insights.so_what: Crypto-native venues are now direct competitors to retail brokerages; asset-to-asset swap UX is the wedge to watch for brokerage share loss.
insights.quote: So, there's 4,000 different uh stocks and ETFs you can buy. You can go straight from Tesla, Apple to Bitcoin back and forth in one step.

insights.claim: Beaton confirms real retail demand for direct asset-to-asset conversion that skips the dollar leg, arguing the reduction in steps and apps is itself an adoption driver rather than a cosmetic feature.
insights.speaker: Nancy Beaton (president of retail, Uphold)
insights.so_what: Validates the decade-old tokenization thesis at the UX layer; friction removal, not ideology, is the adoption variable to monitor.
insights.quote: I want to hit take my Bitcoin and give me Apple.

insights.claim: Uphold pays 3.75% on cash deposits with FDIC insurance up to $2.5 million through a partner bank, plus 3% back on auto-invested paycheck deposits and XRP rewards on debit card spend — using traditional-style incentives to pull deposits onto a crypto platform.
insights.speaker: Nancy Beaton (president of retail, Uphold)
insights.so_what: Crypto platforms are now competing directly with banks on deposit pricing; a deposit-flight vector for regional banks if rates stay above local averages.
insights.quote: you can deposit cash onto the Uphold account and earn 3.75%, which is much higher than the national, you know, local bank average. And through our partner, it's FDIC insured up to 2.5 million.

insights.claim: Beaton names crypto-based IRAs and prediction markets as the next products Uphold's customers are explicitly requesting, with users wanting to migrate from traditional IRAs for the tax advantages.
insights.speaker: Nancy Beaton (president of retail, Uphold)
insights.so_what: Crypto IRA rails and prediction-market infrastructure are the next retail land-grab; tax-advantaged wrappers are stickier AUM than spot balances.

insights.claim: In practice most retail users choose the convenience of centralized custody over holding their own keys, with seed-phrase management being the specific friction that pushes them away from self-custody.
insights.speaker: Nancy Beaton (president of retail, Uphold)
insights.so_what: Undercuts the self-custody thesis for mass-market adoption; centralized venues keep the balances and therefore the monetizable float.
insights.quote: a lot of people choose that convenience over the idea that you, you know, hold your own keys and therefore hold total ownership of your assets

insights.claim: Uphold's answer to the custody tradeoff is Vault, a 2-of-3 multi-key self-custodial wallet where the user holds two keys and Uphold holds one for signing, with key replacement if a user key is lost and instant movement to the exchange to trade.
insights.speaker: Nancy Beaton (president of retail, Uphold)
insights.so_what: Shared-key custody with recovery is the emerging commercial compromise — a design template competitors will likely copy and a threat to pure hardware-wallet vendors.
insights.quote: It has three keys. The user owns two and we have one to sign transactions. So, the user's always in charge.

themes.theme: Clarity Act: an institutional unlock, not a retail one

insights.claim: Beaton frames the Clarity Act's value as removing hesitation specifically for regulated fintechs, broker-dealers and banks — implying retail participation is already proceeding without it.
insights.speaker: Nancy Beaton (president of retail, Uphold)
insights.so_what: Passage should be traded as a catalyst for regulated-institution entry and B2B infrastructure, not as a retail-volume event.
insights.quote: the idea of having, you know, regulatory clarity through the Clarity Act would allow or unblock some of the hesitation on the regulated fintech, broker-dealer, you know, bank enterprise side

insights.claim: Regulators and policymakers have already issued more guidance to trading venues and platforms this year than ever before, so the industry has not been idle waiting on legislation.
insights.speaker: Nancy Beaton (president of retail, Uphold)
insights.so_what: Reduces the binary risk around the Clarity Act — the incremental regulatory path is already de-risking the sector regardless of legislative outcome.
insights.quote: So, there's been uh more guidance than we've ever had before and I think it has continued to help accelerate the space.

insights.claim: Pompliano argues Bitcoin specifically has no need for the Clarity Act because its regulatory status is already settled, separating Bitcoin's risk profile from the rest of the crypto asset complex.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano (host)
insights.so_what: Supports a pair trade: legislative headlines should move altcoins and regulated intermediaries far more than Bitcoin.
insights.quote: I keep hearing about the Clarity Act, and I joke that uh Bitcoin doesn't need the Clarity Act cuz Bitcoin's got clarity.

insights.claim: Beaton's single biggest stated worry is not regulation or price but that media sensationalism and headline noise will overshadow blockchain's operational benefits and slow adoption.
insights.speaker: Nancy Beaton (president of retail, Uphold)
insights.so_what: Suggests the operator-level risk is timeline slippage rather than existential — argues for duration tolerance over tactical timing.
insights.quote: it's not timing the market, it's time in the market

themes.theme: The over-indexed but low-risk crypto holder

insights.claim: Uphold's user data contradicts the stereotype that heavy crypto allocation equals high risk tolerance: a large share of users hold a large portion of their financial portfolio in crypto while being conservative, conviction-driven investors rather than degenerate traders.
insights.speaker: Nancy Beaton (president of retail, Uphold)
insights.so_what: Implies stickier, less flow-sensitive retail balances than models assume — supports lower expected outflow beta during drawdowns.
insights.quote: I think people assume that because you over index in crypto, you're high risk. That's not technically the case. You can over index in crypto, but not be high risk.

insights.claim: A next generation of users treats digital assets the way prior generations treated cash — never having used checks, questioning why banks require physical visits, and expecting money to move like a message.
insights.speaker: Nancy Beaton (president of retail, Uphold)
insights.so_what: Generational default-to-digital implies structural deposit and brokerage share shift over a decade, not a cycle.
insights.quote: I have kids. They don't have checks. They don't have email, right? They wonder why I go to a bank.

themes.theme: Tokenized securities: real but slower than hyped

insights.claim: Pompliano's product-market-fit scorecard ranks Bitcoin, stablecoins and perps as having achieved PMF, while tokenized securities have only promise and remain in the early innings.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano (host)
insights.so_what: A screening framework for allocation: fund the proven PMF categories and treat tokenization exposure as venture-stage optionality.
insights.quote: I would say Bitcoin has product market fit. I'd say stable coins have product market fit. I would say tokenized securities has the promise, but still we're in the early innings. I think perps have product market fit.

insights.claim: Beaton's nearest thing to a bearish call is on timing: moving traditional financial products onto the blockchain will take longer than people expect, partly because those products were built for Monday-to-Friday trading while blockchain rails are 24/7.
insights.speaker: Nancy Beaton (president of retail, Uphold)
insights.so_what: Argues for patience on tokenization-levered equities; near-term revenue from RWA narratives is likely to disappoint versus announcements.
insights.quote: I think getting more of these traditional financial products onto the blockchain might just take a little bit more time than maybe people expect.

insights.claim: Uphold has already announced a tokenized-securities platform partner and expects to ship tokenized securities — including access to private companies — by the end of this year.
insights.speaker: Nancy Beaton (president of retail, Uphold)
insights.so_what: A datable near-term catalyst; retail access to private-company exposure via tokenization is a competitive threat to existing pre-IPO secondary platforms.
insights.quote: by the end of the year, you'll see us, um, have done more with tokenized securities. So, whether that's access to, uh, you know, private companies

insights.claim: Beaton predicts the DeFi-versus-traditional-versus-blockchain product distinction will stop mattering entirely as all financial products migrate to blockchain rails and 24/7 borderless access becomes the baseline expectation.
insights.speaker: Nancy Beaton (president of retail, Uphold)
insights.so_what: If the category label collapses, valuation premia for 'crypto-native' branding compress and execution/distribution become the differentiator.
insights.quote: I think none of that will matter. I think it will all move to the blockchain

themes.theme: Uphold's pivot from retail wallet to white-label infrastructure

insights.claim: Uphold's ten-year strategy is to be known less for its retail wallet and more as the fully API'd platform powering banks, broker-dealers, payment companies and fintechs, which it claims can be stood up for an enterprise client in a matter of weeks.
insights.speaker: Nancy Beaton (president of retail, Uphold)
insights.so_what: Signals the retail crypto app category is commoditizing and margin is migrating to B2B infrastructure — a competitive read-across to other consumer exchanges.
insights.quote: they can have a ready-made platform in a matter of weeks for their end customers

insights.claim: Uphold builds product almost entirely from direct user research — surveys, focus groups, conference and airport conversations — which Pompliano notes is a distinguishing pattern across every Uphold executive he has interviewed.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano (host) and Nancy Beaton
insights.so_what: Explains why Uphold's roadmap tracks retail demand signals closely — its product announcements are a useful leading indicator of what retail crypto users want next.
